title: LLM Judges Can't Separate Trust from Truth
hook: Ask a judge model for a trust score and a correctness verdict and you get two numbers — but they're not two pieces of evidence. Change the source label and both move.
key_points: LLM-as-Judge setups often emit trustworthiness, reliability and factuality scores treated as independent signals.
On correctness-controlled QA, judges align trust scores with truth verdicts more tightly than a human behavioral reference does.
Stress test: hold the QA identical and change only the source cue — labeled Human vs. labeled AI.
That relabeling shifts trust scores, truth verdicts, and logit-derived correct-side probabilities alike.
Conclusion: trust scores should not be read as independent evidence for a truth judgment.
content_html: A common evaluation pattern asks a judge model for several ratings at once — is this trustworthy, is this factually correct — and then treats them as independent readings. Xin Sun and colleagues check whether that holds for the most common pair: a continuous trust score and a binary truth classification. On correctness-controlled QA, the judges bind the two together more tightly than a human behavioral reference does.
extra_html: The stress test makes the coupling concrete. Keeping the QA pair identical and varying only whether the answer is attributed to a human or to an AI, the authors find that source attribution moves not just trust scores but the truth verdicts themselves, and the logit-derived probability mass on the correct side with them. Their recommendation for anyone building evaluation harnesses: do not treat a judge's trust score as independent evidence for its factuality call. Paper on arXiv.

related.title: Inside the Unfair Judge: A Mechanistic Account of LLM-as-Judge Bias
related.hook: LLM judge bias isn't just noisy scoring — it has a geometric signature in hidden states you can find, steer, and use to predict failures on benchmarks you've never tested.

related.title: Can LLMs Judge Better Than They Generate?
related.hook: LLM-as-a-Judge assumes evaluation is easier than generation — a controlled test finds the opposite on 3 of 4 benchmarks, and attention analysis shows why.

related.title: Brand as Memory: VLMs Trust the Masthead, Not the Evidence
related.hook: Show a VLM the same article under a trusted outlet's logo versus an unknown one, and its verdict swings by 1.8x — a bias localized to three specific layers and steerable away.

flashcards.prompt: What assumption about multi-dimensional LLM-as-Judge output does this paper test?
flashcards.back_html: That separate scores — trustworthiness, reliability, factuality — constitute independent evidence, rather than one underlying judgment reported several ways.

flashcards.prompt: What happened when the researchers changed only the source cue (Human vs. AI) on identical QA?

choices.text: Trust scores, truth verdicts, and logit-derived correct-side probabilities all shifted
Trust scores shifted but truth verdicts stayed stable
Nothing changed, since the content was identical
Only the logit probabilities moved, not the stated verdicts

flashcards.explanation_html: Source attribution leaked into the factual judgment itself, not just the perceived trustworthiness — which is why the two scores can't be treated as independent.

flashcards.prompt: How did LLM judges compare to the human behavioral reference on trust–truth coupling?
flashcards.back_html: The models coupled trust scores and truth verdicts more tightly than humans did — weaker separation between the two kinds of judgment.
